newsitem.title: USA: Soyinka calls Nigerian leader "murderous imbecile".
newsitem.headline: Soyinka calls Nigerian leader "murderous imbecile".

text.p: Exiled Nobel literature laureate Wole Soyinka on Sunday denied involvement with a spate of recent bombings in Nigeria and called the country's military leader a "murderous imbecile."
Soyinka, a leading opponent of Nigerian military leader Sani Abacha, and 11 other dissidents were charged with treason on Wednesday by the military government over the recent bombings.
They face the death penalty if convicted.
Speaking by telephone with National Public Radio from Ontario, Canada, Soyinka said the Nigerian government was also harassing his friends and family in Nigeria. He declined to condemn the bombings.

"This is the first time this have ever happened. I've had clashes with regimes before but it has never extended to really menace my family and friends and colleagues in this way," said the 1986 Nobel Prize winner.
He said a group of people active in a student organisation were rounded up by the military government and put in prison simply because he is a patron of the group.

The radical playwright and novelist, who fled to Europe and the United States more than two years ago, strongly condemned Abacha's regime in a 1996 book entitled "The Open Sore of a Continent: A Personal Narrative of the Nigerian Crisis."
Soyinka said he deeply regretted not being able to return to his native country simply because of "some murderous imbecile who has taken over the reins in my country."

Along with Soyinka, others charged in absentia at a Lagos magistrate court were some exiled leaders of the opposition group NADECO, including former army chief Lt. Gen. Alani Akinrinade and wartime Information Minister Anthony Enahoro.
Soyinka said he had been the target of army assassination attempts in the past, and had accepted that as "part of the occupational risk" of being a pro-democracy activist.

He told NPR he had not heightened any security arrangements, although he had increased his life insurance policy "so at least others will have something to fall upon if something should happen to me suddenly."

But he did not go about daily life with a cautious eye over his shoulder. "Having left Nigeria, I cannot now make myself a prisoner to Abacha," he said. "That would render my activities, my creative work totally meaningless."

Soyinka and other pro-democracy activists are fighting for Abacha's annulment of 1993 elections to be reversed and for Moshood Abiola, who took a commanding lead in that vote, to be freed and installed as president. Abiola was jailed in 1994 when he declared himself president.

Nigeria's government has been shunned by the United States and other Western governments since the 1995 hanging of writer Ken Saro Wiwa and eight other minority activists after a special court convicted them of murder.
